relationship: the Lord located in His holy sanctuary
rationale: Habakkuk contrasts mute idols with the Lord in His holy sanctuary. The psalm likewise places the Lord in His holy temple, with His throne in heaven and eyes examining people. Both explicitly identify His holy dwelling, while Habakkuk calls the earth to reverence.
source_text: But the Lord is in His holy sanctuary; let all the earth revere Him.”

target_units.text: The Lord is in His holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven. His eyes look toward the needy; His eyelids examine the sons of men.

relationship: mercy remembered in the face of divine wrath
rationale: Habakkuk declares that God will remember mercy in wrath when his soul is troubled. The psalm likewise asks whether God will forget pity or shut His compassions in wrath, then recalls the Lord's works. This connection concerns mercy and wrath, without interpreting the two living creatures.
source_text: Lord, I have heard Thy report and was afraid; I considered Thy works and was astonished. In the midst of two living creatures Thou wilt be known; when the years draw near Thou wilt be recognized; when the season arrives Thou wilt be revealed. When my soul is troubled, in wrath Thou wilt remember mercy.

target_units.text: “Will the Lord reject for the ages, and not again take pleasure?
Or will He cut off His mercy to the end, from generation to generation?
Or will God forget to show pity, or hold His compassions shut in His wrath?” Diapsalma.
And I said, “Now I have begun; this is the change of the Most High’s right hand.”
I remembered the Lord’s works, for I will remember Thy wonders from the beginning,

relationship: divine appearance described as coming from a mountain region
rationale: Habakkuk depicts God coming from Teman and the Holy One from a shaded mountain, with excellence covering heaven. Deuteronomy likewise describes the Lord coming from Sinai, appearing from Seir and hastening from Mount Paran. The mountain-coming pattern is shared without equating the named locations.
source_text: God will come from Teman, the Holy One from a mountain shaded and thickly wooded. Diapsalma. His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of His praise.

target_units.text: And he said, The Lord has come from Sinai, and appeared unto us from Seir, and hastened from Mount Paran with myriads of Kadesh; at His right hand were angels with Him.
And He spared His people; and all the consecrated ones are under Thy hands; and these are under Thee; and the people received from His words

relationship: brightness in the description of divine glory
rationale: Habakkuk describes divine brightness like light, followed by horns in His hands and mighty love. Ezekiel likewise depicts brightness around the visible likeness of the Lord's glory, comparing it to a bow in cloud. The link concerns radiance, without treating the other visionary details as identical.
source_text: His brightness will be like light; horns are in His hands, and He established mighty love of His strength.

target_units.text: I saw something like the sight of electrum from the appearance of a waist upward; and from the appearance of a waist down below I saw something like the appearance of fire, with its brightness all around.

Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

relationship: earth and mountains shaken and peoples melted before God
rationale: Habakkuk describes the earth shaking, nations melting and mountains crushed. Nahum likewise depicts mountains and earth shaken, rulers melted by fury and rocks crushed. Both present divine presence through these combined images of shaking, melting and crushing.
source_text: He stood, and the earth shook; He looked, and nations melted. Mountains were crushed violently; everlasting hills melted.

target_units.text: Mountains shook before Him and hills were shaken; the whole earth recoiled before Him, and all who dwell in it.
Who will stand before His anger? Who will resist His furious wrath? His fury melts rulers, and rocks were crushed before Him.

relationship: terror and flight in Midian's camp
rationale: Habakkuk says the tents of Midian will be terrified. Judges narrates panic and flight in the camp identified earlier as Midian's, with the Lord setting swords against neighbors. The narrative supplies a particular example of Midianite camp terror, without asserting that Habakkuk identifies this event exclusively.
source_text: I saw His everlasting journeys in place of toils; the dwellings of Ethiopians will be terrified, and the tents of the land of Midian.

target_units.text: Gideon and the hundred men with him entered a section of the camp as the middle watch began. He thoroughly roused the guards, and they sounded the horn trumpets and dashed the jars in their hands.

The three companies sounded the horn trumpets and shattered the jars. They grasped the torches in their left hands, with the horn trumpets in their right hands to sound them, and cried, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”
Each stood by himself around the camp. The whole camp ran; they sounded the alarm and fled.

The three hundred horn trumpets sounded, and the Lord set each man’s sword against his neighbour throughout the camp. The camp fled as far as Beth-shittah and, gathered together, as far as the edge of Abel-meholah and toward Tabbath.

relationship: salvation associated with God's passage through waters
rationale: Habakkuk questions fury against rivers and sea and calls God's riding salvation. The psalm recalls the redemption of His people, fearful waters and depths, and His way in the sea. Both combine divine passage through waters with the people's deliverance.
source_text: Wast Thou angry with rivers, Lord? Was Thy fury against rivers, or Thine onrush against the sea, that Thou wilt mount Thy horses and Thy riding is salvation?

target_units.text: With Thine arm Thou didst redeem Thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Diapsalma.
The waters saw Thee, God; the waters saw Thee and feared, and the depths were troubled—a multitude of sounding waters.
The clouds gave voice, for Thine arrows too pass through.
Thy thunder’s voice was in the wheel; Thy flashes of lightning shone upon the inhabited world; the earth shook and became trembling.
Thy way is in the sea, and Thy paths in many waters, and Thy tracks will not be known.

relationship: God depicted bending a bow for judgment
rationale: Habakkuk pictures God bending His bow against scepters. The psalm likewise presents God as righteous judge and describes Him bending a bow and preparing deadly arrows. The martial image portrays divine judgment, with different objects specified.
source_text: Thou wilt surely bend Thy bow against scepters, says the Lord. Diapsalma. The earth will be torn apart by rivers.

target_units.text: God is a righteous judge, strong and patient, not bringing wrath every day.
If you do not return, He will polish His sword; He bent His bow and prepared it,
and in it He prepared instruments of death; He fashioned His arrows for those being burned.

relationship: waters and depths described with sound during divine appearance
rationale: Habakkuk combines peoples' travail, scattered waters and the abyss giving voice in God's passage. The psalm likewise portrays waters seeing God in fear, troubled depths, sounding waters and clouds giving voice. Both animate the waters in the depiction of divine appearance.
source_text: Peoples will see Thee and travail, as He scatters waters in His passage. The abyss gave its voice, the height of its appearance.

target_units.text: The waters saw Thee, God; the waters saw Thee and feared, and the depths were troubled—a multitude of sounding waters.
The clouds gave voice, for Thine arrows too pass through.
Thy thunder’s voice was in the wheel; Thy flashes of lightning shone upon the inhabited world; the earth shook and became trembling.

relationship: sun and moon within an account of divine battle
rationale: Habakkuk describes the sun raised, the moon standing in its appointed place and bright weapons. Joshua's battle account likewise names the sun standing and the moon remaining still while the Lord fights for Israel. The common celestial and battle setting is retained, while Habakkuk's sun-raised wording is not changed.
source_text: The sun was raised, and the moon stood in its appointed place. Thy missiles will go into light, into the brightness of Thy flashing weapons.

target_units.text: Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day God handed the Amorites over to Israel, when He crushed them at Gibeon and they were crushed before the sons of Israel. Joshua said, “Let the sun stand over Gibeon, and the moon over the ravine of Aijalon.”
The sun stood, and the moon remained still, until God repelled their enemies. The sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not advance toward sunset for a full day.
There was no such day before or afterward, when God listened to a human being, for the Lord fought alongside Israel.

rationale: Habakkuk describes nations brought down in divine fury and earth diminished by threat. Isaiah likewise summons nations and earth to hear because the Lord's wrath and anger are against nations to hand them to slaughter. Both explicitly connect judgment upon nations with divine fury.
source_text: With threat Thou wilt diminish the earth, and in fury Thou wilt bring nations down.

target_units.text: Draw near, nations, and hear, rulers! Let the earth and those in it hear, the inhabited world and the people in it!
For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.

relationship: salvation and mercy for God's anointed
rationale: Habakkuk describes God going out to save His people and His anointed ones. The psalm likewise magnifies His king's salvations and mercy to His anointed, David and his seed. The connection preserves the source's plural anointed ones and the psalm's specifically named royal recipient.
source_text: Thou didst go out for Thy people’s salvation, to save Thine anointed ones. Thou didst cast death upon the heads of lawless people and didst raise bonds up to the neck. Diapsalma.

target_units.text: magnifying the salvations of His king and showing mercy to His anointed, to David and to his seed for ever.

relationship: God's way through the sea's waters
rationale: Habakkuk pictures God's horses driven into the sea and troubling much water. The psalm likewise describes God's way in the sea and paths in many waters. Both portray divine movement through water, without assigning horses to the psalm.
source_text: Thou didst drive Thy horses into the sea as they troubled much water.

target_units.text: Thy way is in the sea, and Thy paths in many waters, and Thy tracks will not be known.

relationship: bodily distress in response to a prophetic encounter
rationale: Habakkuk describes terror in his belly, trembling in his bones and a troubled bodily condition. Daniel likewise describes strong fear surrounding the vision and his own loss of strength and fall to the ground. Both describe the bodily effect of the encounter, with distinct sensations and accounts of sound.
source_text: I kept watch, and my belly was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips. Trembling entered my bones, and my bodily condition beneath me was troubled. I will rest on a day of affliction, to go up to the people of my sojourning.

target_units.text: I, Daniel, saw this great vision, but the men with me did not see it. Strong fear fell upon them, and they fled in haste.
I was left alone and saw this great vision. No strength remained in me; a spirit turned upon me for destruction, and I had no strength.
I did not hear the sound of his speech; I had fallen face down upon the earth.

relationship: failure of fields, vines and fig trees
rationale: Habakkuk lists failed figs, vines, olives and fields producing no food. Joel likewise describes failed grain, diminished oil and dried or diminished vines, figs and field trees. Both enumerate agricultural loss across several crops.
source_text: For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and vines will have no produce; the olive’s labor will fail, and fields will not produce food. Sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no cattle at feeding troughs.

target_units.text: because the plains have suffered. Let the earth mourn, because grain has suffered, wine has dried up, and oil has diminished.
The farmers have dried up. Lament, estates, over wheat and barley, because the harvest from the field has perished.
The vine has dried up and the fig trees have diminished; pomegranate, palm, apple tree and all the field’s trees have dried up, because human beings have put joy to shame.

rationale: Habakkuk describes sheep failing for lack of food and no cattle at feeding troughs. Joel likewise says cattle have no pasture and sheep disappeared. The animals' food failure is a distinct shared element of the agricultural calamity.
source_text: For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and vines will have no produce; the olive’s labor will fail, and fields will not produce food. Sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no cattle at feeding troughs.

target_units.text: What shall we store up for ourselves? Herds of cattle wept because they had no pasture, and flocks of sheep disappeared.

rationale: Habakkuk declares that he will exult in the Lord and rejoice in God his Savior. Mary's song likewise magnifies the Lord and says her spirit rejoiced in God her Savior. The closely corresponding declaration links the two songs.
source_text: But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Savior.

target_units.text: Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior,

relationship: God's strength places the speaker's feet upon heights
rationale: Habakkuk names God as his strength, setting his feet toward completion and leading him onto heights. The psalm likewise describes divine power, a blameless way, firmly set feet and standing on heights. The shared cluster is retained without importing the psalm's deer comparison into Habakkuk.
source_text: The Lord God is my strength; He will set my feet toward completion and lead me onto the heights, to conquer in His song.

target_units.text: God girds me with power and made my way blameless,
He sets my feet firmly like a deer’s and makes me stand upon the heights,
training my hands for war; and Thou madest my arms a bronze bow.
